source.title: Showing SAE Latents Are Not Atomic Using Meta-SAEs

page_placements.theme: Feature composition and cross-method granularity at a fixed dictionary size

record.tranche_reason: The study reports its own decompositions and comparisons that argue SAE latents need not be atomic, refining the interpretation of feature splitting.
record.gate_note: The post also reports city-attribute steering results, but those test editing behavior rather than the feature-splitting and latent-relationship claims. Cited results from other work are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The post reports its own GPT-2-small layer-8 results showing that larger-SAE latents decompose into sparse, interpretable components (meta-latents and smaller-SAE latents), and that split latents share a parent component. It uses this to argue SAE latents are not atomic, which bears on V1, V3 and V5.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude SAE latents are monosemantic but not atomic: they are common compositions of more basic units, shown by sparse interpretable meta-SAE decompositions. They also conclude meta-SAEs often recover split-feature structure and allow finer city-attribute steering. They caution that meta-latents are lossy, not the true or maximally atomic units, and that smaller SAEs may give similar insights.
record.recipe_differences: Rather than measuring only feature splitting across ordinary SAE dictionary sizes, the study trains an SAE on SAE decoder directions and uses its decompositions to analyze latent relationships and splits.
record.method_sensitivity: The comparison uses a cosine-similarity threshold of > 0.7 to identify split latents; the post also notes that results and relationships differ between meta-SAE and smaller-SAE comparisons.

fits_no_version.finding: Meta-SAE latents relate SAE-49152 latents differently from cosine similarity with SAE-3072 latents: 28.92% overlap at matched edge counts. Many meta-latents have no close SAE-49152 match but often have one in SAE-3072.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Decompositions of large-SAE latents depend on the decomposition method (meta-SAE vs smaller SAE).

fits_no_version.finding: Smaller-SAE latents activate fewer meta-latents on average. The authors attribute this to smaller-SAE-like latents recurring across sizes in the meta-SAE training set.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Meta-SAE structure across SAE sizes reflects training-set frequency artifacts.

record.problems: The authors describe the work as preliminary and limited to one small model, one layer, one meta-SAE, and a small set of qualitative examples. They note that the examples are slightly cherry-picked, that the meta-SAE decomposition is lossy, and that more rigorous evaluation is needed.
record.rows_left_out: The post includes additional illustrative SAE-latent case studies and a city-attribute steering experiment. The latter measures editing behavior rather than the claim versions recorded here; further examples do not add a separately quantified test of the claim.

untested.parts: Whether split latents cover or partition the parent's inputs. Only one split example is shown; there is no systematic count across features.
Large models and open SAE releases. Gemma Scope work is mentioned as exploratory, with no results reported.
Whether families mirror a concept hierarchy in the model's representation beyond one example. The authors leave open whether relations are a hierarchy or a cyclic graph.
Entirely untested: no parent-firing or absorption measurement, and no size or sparsity sweep for absorption.
Whether larger SAEs add novel latents absent from smaller ones. Whether any dictionary size yields a complete atomic set.
Entirely untested: no comparison of training objectives and no Matryoshka SAEs.

missing.what: Reconstruction test: replace meta-SAE decoders with the max-cosine latents from four SAEs (SAE-768 to SAE-6144), fine-tune the encoder, and compare with random directions. The result is only slightly worse than the original meta-SAE, which shows larger-SAE latents are sparsely reconstructible from smaller-SAE latents.
missing.locator: Are Meta-Latents different from SAE Latents?; reconstruction-variant paragraph

missing.what: Claim that a meta-SAE trained on the larger SAE 'often recovers' split structure, stated as a key result with no quantified rate.
missing.locator: TL;DR key results; Using Meta-SAEs to Interpret Split Features

record.verdict_notes: Preliminary LessWrong post: one model, one layer, one meta-SAE, and cherry-picked qualitative examples. The same authors later wrote arXiv:2502.04878, an original source for V5. This post is a distinct earlier study, so verdicts are given, but readers should weigh the non-independence. The city steering results do not bear on any version.

versions.untested_parts: The post does not measure whether the split latents partition or collectively cover the parent latent's inputs. It gives a qualitative example rather than a broad test across features.
The experiments are on GPT-2-small at one layer; the post does not test large models or open SAE releases.
The post gives qualitative examples of shared and more specific meta-latents, but does not establish a general nested hierarchy or systematically measure geometric closeness across feature families.
The post does not test parent-latent firing where child latents take over, or whether changes in SAE size or sparsity resolve absorption.
The comparisons do not establish that larger SAEs systematically decompose into smaller-SAE latents, nor that every dictionary size adds novel latents or lacks a complete atomic set.
The post does not compare training objectives or test whether the SAE objective causes splitting; it does not test Matryoshka SAEs.

rows.subject: GPT-2-small
rows.size_stated: SAE dictionary sizes 24576 and 49152; meta-SAE dictionary size 2304
rows.operation_detail: Compared SAE latents across dictionary sizes using a meta-SAE trained on decoder directions; split latents were identified using cosine similarity > 0.7.
rows.measure: Qualitative change in meta-latents associated with a parent and its split latents
rows.baseline: SAE size 24576 latent 8326 has one active meta-latent, 589, related to talking/speaking.
rows.value: At SAE size 49152, the feature splits into seven latents; the described latents share meta-latent 589 and add more specific meta-latents.
rows.locator: Using Meta-SAEs to Interpret Split Features
rows.note: The post describes examples including noun and sentence-initial uses of “talk,” future-talk phrases, and participial uses. It does not report whether their inputs partition or cover the smaller latent's inputs.
rows.check: The one qualitative example fully shows the pattern. A 24576 latent splits into seven 49152 latents, each at cosine > 0.7 and each sharing meta-latent 589. It should be observed for the parts it measures, not partial. Input coverage is untested and is listed as untested rather than lowering the state.

source_check.correct: Latent 8326 (SAE-24576) has only meta-latent 589. The text says it splits into 7 SAE-49152 latents but lists only 6: 37123, 23912, 10563, 12210, 25593 and 46174. All 6 have meta-latent 589. Five add more meta-latents; 12210 has only 589. Split latents are identified at cosine > 0.7. The split analysis uses a separate meta-SAE trained on 8 SAE sizes (768 to 98304), not the 2304-latent one.
source_check.locator_found: Using Meta-SAEs to Interpret Split Features, talk example and footnote 1
source_check.problem: Row is fine as worded ('the described latents'). Only 6 of the 7 children are listed, and 12210 adds no meta-latent.

rows.subject: GPT-2-small
rows.size_stated: SAE-49152 and SAE-3072; meta-SAE dictionary size 2304
rows.operation_detail: Compared meta-latent decoder directions with SAE latent directions using cosine similarity.
rows.measure: Whether a meta-latent has a cosine-similar SAE latent
rows.baseline: Cosine similarity > 0.7 is described as the threshold for a very similar latent.
rows.value: For many meta-latents there is no very similar latent in SAE-49152, while there often is one in SAE-3072.
rows.locator: Are Meta-Latents different from SAE Latents?; distributions of maximum cosine similarities
rows.note: The post gives this as a qualitative summary of plots, without reporting counts. Meta-latents are not themselves SAE latents, so this is evidence about related decompositions rather than a direct count of novel features in a larger SAE.
rows.check: Compares meta-latent directions with SAE latents. This characterises the study's tool, not whether larger-SAE latents decompose or whether novel latents appear.

rows.operation_detail: Compared qualitative decompositions of the SAE-49152 Einstein latent using meta-latents and high-cosine SAE latents.
rows.measure: Interpretable concepts represented in alternative latent decompositions
rows.value: Meta-latents include science and scientists, prominent figures, cosmic and astronomical terms, German names and locations, electricity and energy, and capital-E words. The SAE-3072 comparison includes physics/economics/math, science and scientists, prominent figures, Germany/Germans, and astronomical terms.

rows.note: A qualitative case study. The post says the SAE-3072 latents give a similar decomposition, though some are more specific.

The authors note the meta-SAE decomposition is lossy and the examples slightly cherry-picked. It is not a hierarchy test for V3, since it shows composition of attributes, not a nested parent/child family.
